schools.summary: Gregory the Great reads the flat formula as the reflex of a man losing an argument, repeating what all know lest he seem defeated; by comparison with God our knowledge is ignorance, and all we do well we do to ourselves, not to God (Ps. 16:2).

Henry sorts a true doctrine from a false aim: Eliphaz's insinuation that Job thought God unjust is a strained innuendo, yet the principle that God is no man's debtor (Rom. 11:35) is sound in itself and cruel in its use.
Gill: Eliphaz, first and oldest, leads every course, but here betakes himself to calumny and reproach instead of solid reasons for conviction.
Ellicott marks a far more exaggerated and offensive tone, accusing Job of specific crimes, opening from the axiom that God's judgment must be wholly disinterested.

Keil and Delitzsch trace the verb sakan (peculiar to Job), from the Hiph. of ch. 21:21 — to dwell beside, grow accustomed, be serviceable — rendering 'the intelligent man is profitable to himself,' the same root returning at v.21; Ellicott takes 'as he that is wise' as an independent statement.
Gill: no man, even the best, can profit God; the good man's goodness extends not to the Lord — 'we are unprofitable servants.'
Clarke: a man may profit a man but none his Maker; 'thy iniquities are against justice.' Wesley reads it a rebuke of self-importance — 'as if thou didst oblige God by it.'

themes: can a man be profitable to God

schools.summary: Gill will not press the negation into a denial of all complacency: God does take pleasure in his people as righteous in Christ, in the graces of his Spirit and their prayers — yet this adds no new pleasure, for he would have had as much delight within himself had there never been a holy angel or a righteous man.

Clarke: God, infinite in perfection, can neither gain nor lose by men's righteousness or sin. Wesley: not such a pleasure as he needs for his own contentment — 'we are undone without him, but he is happy without us.'

themes: is it pleasure to the Almighty
pleasure in the righteous for Christ's sake
a comfort turned to a taunt

schools.summary: Henry: God does not reprove out of fear or jealousy, as princes curb a growing subject; he rebukes the good because he loves them, never the great because he fears them — Pharaoh and Herod oppressed from fear, but God perverts no justice for fear of any.

Gill: God chastises not for fear of hurt, being in no danger of dethronement; but records Broughton's rendering 'for thy fear,' i.e. for thy piety, granting that good men who fear God are yet afflicted.
Ellicott glosses 'because he standeth in awe of thee — will he justify his dealings with thee?'

Clarke reads a sarcasm — is God afraid thou wilt injure him, that he stripped thee? Wesley: not from fear lest thou grow too great — 'as thy righteousness cannot profit him, so thy wickedness can do him no hurt.'

debates.question: Does the verse mean 'for fear of thee' (God's dread of Job) or 'for thy fear' (for Job's piety)?

sides.position: God's supposed dread of Job — 'will he reprove thee for fear of thee?'
'for thy fear' — that is, for thy fear of God, thy piety/religion

themes: will he reprove thee for fear of thee
no motive to afflict but justice

schools.summary: Henry marks the moment the mask comes off — 'Thou art the man'; nothing is infinite but God, yet sin against Infinite Majesty has a kind of infinite malignity; and he turns on Eliphaz, whose slander wronged Job as much as the Sabeans, for a good name is more precious than wealth.
Gill owns that every heart's wickedness is great and all sin great as against God, yet insists the general truth is here wrongly fastened on a particular man.
Clarke reads the Hebrew — 'of thy continuance in them there is no end' (ein kets) — charging not only many great sins but obstinate persistence.

Ellicott exposes the root fallacy: mere conjecture from the false assumption that a just God can only punish the wicked, so those he punishes must be wicked — the very axiom the book exists to overthrow.

themes: slander as its own great sin

schools.summary: Henry lays out the charge as Eliphaz frames it — a pledge of great value seized from a brother, the LXX's 'thy brethren for pledges,' the poor stripped of the very clothes the law of Moses forbade to keep overnight (Exod. 22:26; Deut. 24:13).

Gill weighs 'for nought' as a trifling sum or a short loan needing no pledge; records the rendering 'thy brothers for a pledge' (their persons); and presses the moral point — conjecture uncharitable, assertion false.
Ellicott: these specific charges, false as they were, show the depth to which Eliphaz had sunk.
Clarke: Job vexatious, exacting where nothing was due, so the poor could not clothe themselves. Wesley hears strong presumption — 'when I consider thy calamities, I conclude thou art guilty.'

themes: a pledge taken from a brother

schools.summary: Gill feels the smallness of the thing denied — a cup of cold water, one of the least favours, refused to a weary desert traveller; inhuman, and far from Job's real character.
Henry presses the charge from Eliphaz's side: not so much as cold water to the weary, and bread withheld from the hungry — to withhold good from those to whom it is due (Prov. 3:27).
Keil and Delitzsch see the whole portrait: the 'man of the arm' is Job himself, imagined to have engrossed the land by violence or cunning, the all-absorbing love of self ruling all his dealings.
Clarke supplies the custom — giving water to thirsty travellers a great Eastern virtue, the Indian devotees standing on the roads with skins of water — that makes the accusation bite.

themes: a real virtue turned to slander

schools.summary: Clarke unpacks ish zeroa, 'the man of arm' — of power, rapine, and plunder — and 'the man whose face is accepted,' the man of wealth: 'thou wert an enemy to the poor but didst flatter the rich.' Wesley: 'dwelt' — by thy sentence he had sure possession, right or no.
Gill makes the mighty man a third party Job favoured as judge, giving the disputed land to the rich against the poorer.

Keil and Delitzsch make the arm-man Job himself, who looked on the land as his and filled it out alone, crowding all others out; Ellicott concurs it is probably Job, setting aside the notion that vv.5ff are God's words.

debates.question: Is 'the mighty man' a rich party Job favoured, or Job himself the oppressor?

sides.position: a rich third party whom Job, as judge, unjustly favoured
Job himself, the arm-man who devoured his neighbours' land

themes: the mighty man had the earth

schools.summary: Gill: widows turned from a rich man's door or a magistrate's court, sent away with neither food nor redress.
Henry notes the blackest stroke slipped in by insinuation — 'the arms of the fatherless have been broken,' not quite 'thou hast broken them,' yet those in power who fail to relieve are chargeable.
Keil and Delitzsch carry it to the doom Eliphaz draws: on account of this inhuman action snares are round about him (cf. Bildad, ch. 18:8-10), ruin on every side, terrors coming suddenly.
Clarke: whatever the fatherless had, Job is charged with stripping — enriched with the spoils of the defenceless. Wesley glosses 'arms' as 'their supports and rights.'

themes: the completed portrait of the oppressor

schools.summary: Gill fastens on 'therefore': because of the charged sins, punishments beset Job on every side — the Sabeans, the fire, the wind, the boils — the ruin offered as proof of the guilt.
Clarke draws out the retribution: as Job spoiled, so is he spoiled, taken in a net; a vivid image of the elephant hunted from strait to strait into a narrowing enclosure.
Henry hears it reach the conscience: providence crosses such men with snares, and no sin makes a louder inward cry than unmercifulness — 'sudden fear troubleth thee.'
Keil and Delitzsch confirm the note of terror: the coming ruin makes itself felt in alarms that seize the guilty man suddenly and disconcert him.

themes: therefore snares are round about thee
a syllogism built on false premises

schools.summary: Gill offers the darkness two ways — a judicial blindness of mind, or the darkness of affliction whose cause cannot be seen — and owns the latter was truly Job's case, sitting in inward and outward darkness alike.

Clarke suspects a lost letter — 'or' (au) was originally 'light' (aur), so LXX 'thy light is changed into darkness'; Houbigant emends to 'darkness, and not light, shalt thou behold.' Wesley: fear of further evils, or the gross darkness of present misery, 'waters' a flood of afflictions.
Keil and Delitzsch weigh 'thou canst not see,' refusing a merely circumstantial sense and holding the line open between affirmative and interrogative.
Henry: the guilty man at his wits' end, set as in a mist amid dark waters; those who show no mercy may justly be denied the hope of mercy.

outliers.note: Proposes a textual emendation — the initial 'or' (au) was originally 'light' (aur), giving the LXX's 'thy light is changed into darkness,' with Houbigant's 'darkness, and not light, shalt thou behold.'

themes: darkness that thou canst not see

schools.summary: Gill dwells on the plain glory — heaven named from its height, God's throne and the seat of his majesty, so that 'heaven' becomes one of his names; renders also 'the height of the heavens' or 'higher than the heavens.'
Henry takes the doctrine at face value: God is in the height of heaven, whence Eliphaz rightly proves a man cannot profit God nor contend with him, and should approach with reverence.

Clarke sees the trap — Eliphaz imputes to Job the infidel inference that God, so exalted behind cloud and ether, cannot see the earth; 'if a man be dressed in a bear's skin, he may be hunted by his own dogs.' Wesley reads the height as the ground of God's oversight, looking down to govern and recompense.
Keil and Delitzsch name the practical atheism of the Psalms (73:11; 94:7), which denies the God of heaven a knowledge of earthly things, as Epicurus his unconcerned gods.

themes: God in the height of heaven
a true confession bent to a charge

schools.summary: Gill: Job never said 'how doth God know?' with his lips; Eliphaz supposed it his heart's reasoning, an invidious consequence from Job's remarks on the prosperity of the wicked, twisted into a denial of providence.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'What doth God know? Can he judge through the thick cloud?' — the charge that Job has joined the scoffers who fence heaven off from earth.

Clarke protests the method — attributing blasphemies Job never held and drawing injurious inferences: 'Job's friends attribute falsities to him,' as polemic writers in theology and politics love to do.
Henry names the sin: to hold the truth in unrighteousness, for bad men expel the fear of God by banishing his eye from the world (Ezek. 8:12).

themes: a creed put in Job's mouth

schools.summary: Gill exposes the false logic — atheists make God like themselves, fancying that as clouds hide the stars from men, they hide men from God; whereas nothing comes between God and man.

Clarke: God confined to his exalted regions, caring nothing for earth's inhabitants. Wesley: the old error of the philosophers — God's delight in heaven, unwilling to burden himself with the care of earth — falsely fathered on Job.

Henry answers both suppositions — that God cannot see through the cloud (absurd, since distance is nothing to him who fills immensity), or that it is below his glory to govern this lower world; if the sun reaches earth from that height, shall we question the Creator (Ps. 19:6)?
Keil and Delitzsch render 'in the vault of heaven he walketh at his pleasure' — a God who strolls the ramparts of the sky heedless of earth.

themes: thick clouds a covering to him
he walketh the circuit of heaven

schools.summary: Gill hears 'the old way' as the ancient course of sin since the fall — the way of Cain and of the old world, the 'world of the ungodly,' a beaten road of iniquity trodden obstinately.

Henry gives it rhetorical force: Eliphaz would frighten Job by the sinners of the old world — the flood and Sodom set together for warning (Luke 17:26; 2 Pet. 2:5-6) — that Job may see his own face in that glass.
Clarke takes it as a fresh accusation — Job walks the same way the wicked of old walked in — with allusion to the Flood; Wesley glosses 'the way of antiquity,' their end or success.
Ellicott renders it accusingly, 'dost thou keep the old way which the wicked men trod? dost thou hold their tenets?'

debates.question: Is the question a warning to mark the old way's end, or a charge that Job walks it?

sides.position: a warning — mark the doom of the old world, that we not walk in it
an accusation — dost thou keep that way, holding their tenets?

themes: the old way of the wicked
the wrong man in the glass

schools.summary: Gill lingers over 'out of time' — sent into eternity before the common term of life, cut off in the midst of days, or 'without time,' suddenly, like trees by the axe or grass by the scythe.
Henry reads their 'foundation' as the earth on which they built their hopes, overflown by the flood; those who build on such sand are swept away when the floods come (Matt. 7:27).
Clarke identifies the unrighteous of Noah's day who said 'Depart from us'; Wesley: destroyed together with their foundation, the earth and all their supports, by the general deluge.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'withered up before their time, their foundation poured out as a stream'; Ellicott ties it to the Flood (weighty for the book's age), but adds a figurative sense — the wicked's principles infectious, bearing all before them like a river.

debates.question: Is 'whose foundation was overflown with a flood' the literal deluge or a figure for infectious principles?

sides.position: the literal earth swept away by Noah's flood
an image of corrupting principles that sweep a generation away like a flowing stream

schools.summary: Gill: the language of men who would not be admonished or governed; Job used the words of prosperous sinners, Eliphaz turns them on men cut off for their wickedness.

Henry weighs 'what can the Almighty do for them?' three ways — the justice of their punishment, the injustice of their sin (Mic. 6:3; Jer. 2:5), or the reason of their sin (Zeph. 1:12) — the absurdity exposed by the one word 'Almighty.'
Clarke sets it in Noah's day — 'Let him do his worst' — noting the LXX's 'to us' for 'to them'; Wesley makes the reversal explicit: Eliphaz repeats Job's words (ch. 21:14-15) 'to a contrary purpose.'
Ellicott: again Eliphaz fathers on Job the thoughts Job ascribed to the wicked; Keil and Delitzsch render 'Depart from us! and what can the Almighty do to them?'

themes: what can the Almighty do for them

schools.summary: Gill reads the first half as the measure of ingratitude: God filled their houses with providential good, and to load with benefits the men who said 'what can the Almighty do?' is the deep aggravation of their contempt.

Clarke shows Eliphaz sarcastically quoting Job's own words (ch. 21:16) — 'thank God I have no part with you nor your creed'; Wesley: he repeats them 'not without reflection — thou didst say so, but against thy own principle.'
Ellicott: the bitterness of the irony reaches its climax, Eliphaz adopting the very formula of repudiation Job had used.
Henry reads it more kindly, a sincere disowning of atheism in which quarrelling friends may unite; and warns that houses full of good things but hearts empty of grace are marked for ruin.

debates.question: Is 'the counsel of the wicked is far from me' a taunt or a sincere repudiation?

sides.position: a barbed taunt, throwing Job's own words back in his teeth
a sincere shared abhorrence of atheism, in which even disputants unite

themes: he filled their houses with good things
the counsel of the wicked far from me

schools.summary: Gill guards the gladness from cruelty: the righteous rejoice not in the misery of fellow-creatures but in being kept from such sins, delivered from such oppressors, and chiefly in the glory of God's holiness and justice.

Keil and Delitzsch set it beside the close of many a psalm where retributive justice at last breaks out to the joy of the innocent (Ps. 58:11); Ellicott refers the sight to the destruction of the wicked as in Noah's day.
Clarke: the righteous see God's judgments and know the Judge of all the earth does right, rejoicing in all the dispensations of his providence.

Henry gives the laughter its holy warrant — gladness not at suffering but at God glorified and oppressors broken, laughing them to scorn as God does (Ps. 2:4; Prov. 1:26); some read it of Noah and Lot.

themes: the righteous see it and are glad
the innocent laugh them to scorn
Job made the object of the scorn

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch read the shout of the innocent — 'verily our opponent is destroyed, and the fire hath devoured their abundance'; Ellicott: 'they that did rise up against us are cut off,' judging the AV less correct.

Clarke paraphrases the righteous kept in peace while the wicked are destroyed to their remnant, noting Good's 'our tribe' for 'our substance' (flood in Noah's day, fire in Lot's); Wesley marks Eliphaz ranking himself among the righteous, 'fire' the burning of Sodom.
Gill allows it may be Eliphaz and his friends contrasting their unbroken estate with Job's, the difference being that they were righteous and he wicked.

Henry hears the friends' self-congratulation — 'our substance is not cut down as thine is; we prosper, a sign we are Heaven's favourites' — a deceitful rule, for none knows love or hatred by all before him.

debates.question: Whose words are 'our substance is not cut down' — the innocent's triumph, or Eliphaz's self-comparison with Job?

sides.position: the triumph-song of the righteous over the destroyed wicked
Eliphaz contrasting his own unbroken estate with Job's ruin

themes: our substance is not cut down
a boast built on a false measure

schools.summary: Henry can 'almost forgive Eliphaz his hard censures' for this counsel — ministers must speak from both Sinai and Sion; acquaint thyself with God, acquiesce, join his interest, and be at peace with thyself and with God, for how can two walk together except they be agreed (Amos 3:3)?
Gill notes the change of temper from charges to advice, still on the false supposition Job is estranged; acquaintance with God begins at conversion, carried on by prayer and worship.

Keil and Delitzsch tie the verb to the sakan of v.2 — 'make friends now with him, so hast thou peace'; Ellicott notes Eliphaz does as he did in ch. 5 and Zophar in ch. 11, reading 'thereby shall thine increase be good.'

Clarke suggests the verb means 'treasure up, lay up' an interest with God; Wesley expands the summons — renew acquaintance by prayer, repentance, humiliation, and compliance, our honour that we are capable of it, our misery that by sin we lost it.

themes: the turn from threat to counsel

schools.summary: Gill doubts the law of Moses is meant (whether it yet was, or reached Job), taking 'the law' as any doctrine or revelation made to the patriarchs and handed down, received as God's word and obeyed.

Henry reads it as the heart of conversion — to receive the law from God's mouth, not the world's ('Lord, what wilt thou have me to do?' Acts 9:6) — and to retain it, laid up in the heart as a thing of price.

Clarke dismisses the Noahic-precepts view — 'stuff and vanity!' — insisting the allusion is plainly to the Law of Moses, the Torah, containing his very words; Wesley: take the rule from God's law written in the mind and the instruction of holy men.

Ellicott inclines the other way — Job being the one Gentile book of the OT, likelier prior to the Law, though he owns the difficulty of 'his words' before Moses, unless the inner voice of God in the conscience; Keil and Delitzsch render 'receive teaching from his mouth, and place his utterances in thy heart.'

debates.question: Does 'the law' (torah) from his mouth mean the Mosaic Law or a pre-Mosaic revelation?

sides.position: the Law afterward given by Moses, the Torah, emphatically
an older patriarchal revelation / the inner voice of God in the conscience

themes: receive the law from his mouth
lay up his words in thine heart
the age and authorship of Job

schools.summary: Gill hears in 'return' the confession of a prior departure, and encouragement in the name Shaddai, the all-sufficient One whose grace suffices to receive, pardon, supply, and preserve returning sinners.

Keil and Delitzsch note 'return unto' (shuv ad) marks a thorough turning, and 'be built up' means prosperity raised again from its ruins (Jer. 24:6); Ellicott: 'thou shalt put away iniquity' implies the imputation of apostasy to Job.

Clarke: God will restore his prosperity and a household of children; Wesley marks the emphatic Hebrew of thorough turning, and weighs the last clause as spiritual (grace to reform) or temporal (the punishment of sin put away).
Henry urges not only to turn from sin but home to God by a universal reformation, and to put away iniquity from the tabernacle (Zophar's advice, ch. 11:14) — family reformation is needful.

themes: if thou return to the Almighty

schools.summary: Gill takes it a promise of plenty — such abundance of gold as not to be counted.
Clarke shows how widely the versions differ (Montanus, Vulgate 'flint for earth, torrents of gold for flint,' Calmet, Good, Coverdale), leaving the drift an increase of treasure.

Ellicott presses the opposite sense — 'put thy treasure on a level with the dust, the gold of Ophir among the stones' — reckon it worthless, do not set thy heart on it; Keil and Delitzsch likewise 'lay by in the dust the gold ore'; Ellicott notes Ophir's site (India, Arabia, Africa) is disputed.

Henry holds both: Job shall lay up gold, yet 'not as his treasure and portion, but as dust,' laying it at his feet not in his bosom — wealth a blessing only when we are not ensnared with the love of it.

debates.question: Does 'lay up gold as dust' promise abundant gold or command Job to esteem gold as worthless dust?

sides.position: a promise of abundant, uncounted gold
a command to reckon gold worthless as dust and put it away

themes: a heart set free from gold

schools.summary: Gill gives both readings — God as defence, a wall of fire securing wealth and soul, or 'the Almighty shall be thy gold,' bidding Job reckon God his truest treasure, grace better than perishing gold (1 Pet. 1:7).
Henry seizes the 'gold' reading for a fine stroke: 'worldlings make gold their god, and saints make God their gold' — the favoured have the best gold and a defence against every Sabean and Chaldean.

Ellicott reads 'the Almighty shall be thy treasure, and precious silver unto thee,' the rare word (cf. 'strength of the hills,' 'of a unicorn') meaning brightness; Keil and Delitzsch: 'gold ore in abundance, and silver of the brightest lustre.'

Clarke keeps the silver plain but challenges the doctrine beneath — that God gives most earthly good to those he loves best, the rich his favourites and the poor his enemies — the false theology of the whole speech.

debates.question: Is the Hebrew word 'thy defence' or 'thy gold / treasure'?

sides.position: 'the Almighty shall be thy defence'
'the Almighty shall be thy gold / thy treasure'

outliers.note: Challenges Eliphaz's underlying theology — that God gives the most earthly good to those he loves best, the rich and great his high favourites, the poor and distressed his enemies.

themes: the Almighty thy defence or thy gold

schools.summary: Gill makes the delight the fruit of a reordered heart — in God's perfections, works, word, and communion — possible only when Job's affections are taken off riches and God is made his gold.

Henry: thus the Almighty becomes Job's gold, by his delighting in him as worldlings in money; the way to our heart's desire is to make God our heart's delight (Ps. 37:4), and then to lift up the face with boldness (1 John 3:21).
Ellicott notes Zophar had promised the same, to lift up the face without spot (ch. 11:15); Keil and Delitzsch render 'delight thyself in the Almighty, and lift up thy countenance to Eloah.'

Wesley: 'look up to him with cheerfulness and confidence.' Clarke halts at the doctrine — making delight turn on restored prosperity is a gospel unlike Paul's and John's, for tribulation itself is often a mark of God's favour.

outliers.note: Faults Eliphaz's prosperity-doctrine as contrary to the gospel of Paul and John — the justified have peace, the Spirit witnesses sonship, and we glory in tribulation, which is itself often a mark of God's favour, not its withdrawal.

themes: lift up thy face to God
God made our gold by delighting in him
prosperity as the wrong evidence of favour

schools.summary: Gill: a supplication pleading not merit but mercy, for the Lord's and Christ's sake, offered often (the word implies multiplying) — a privilege and benefit, the access of a child to a Father through the Mediator.

Clarke unfolds the Hebrew 'thou shalt open,' unbosom thyself — when the heart prays God hears; Wesley: 'thou shalt multiply thy prayer,' sending to heaven for wisdom and strength, and pay the vows by obtaining the blessings sought.
Keil and Delitzsch render 'if thou prayest to him, he will hear thee, and thou shalt pay thy vows,' the first of a chain of blessings running on through the verses to come.
Henry pictures a steady correspondence with heaven — petitions up, answers down — and the paying of vows, for when God performs what we prayed for we must perform what we promised (Ps. 116:14).

Gill guards the words (strictly, only God's decrees are unfrustrable — man appoints, God disappoints) then allows the promise to Job as magistrate, private man, or best of all praying man, whose purposes committed to God are brought to pass.
Clarke: 'whatsoever thou purposest in his strength, thou shalt accomplish'; Wesley: purposes not disappointed but ratified by God, with the light of divine direction, comfort, and success.

Ellicott hears an allusion to Abraham's intercession for Sodom, the decreeing shading into prevailing prayer; Keil and Delitzsch render 'thou devisest a plan, and it shall be established, and light shineth upon thy ways.'
Henry draws the inward calm — frame projects with resignation and the issue is to thy content; commit thy works and thy thoughts are established (Prov. 16:3), the light shining where now is darkness.

themes: the prevailing prayer of the righteous
repose in accord with God's will

schools.summary: Gill takes the cast-down as the wicked brought low from prosperity into straits, against whose fall the returning Job shall stand secure.

Henry reads it inwardly: when men sink toward despair Job shall find that which lifts him above his troubles — when hearts fail for fear, God's disciples lift up their heads for joy (Luke 21:26-28), for God saves the humble.

Clarke renders it a command of faith, 'thou shalt say, Be exalted; for the downcast of eye he will save' — the gospel's humble-exalted; Wesley keeps the kindlier sense, that in a general calamity God will deliver Job.

Keil and Delitzsch take the cry as an imperative — 'thou sayest, Arise! and him that hath low eyes he saveth'; Ellicott records a harsher possibility, 'thou shalt say, It was pride that caused their fall.'

debates.question: What is the temper of Job's saying when men are cast down?

sides.position: a cheerful assurance of exaltation to the humble — 'there is lifting up'
an imperative to the fallen — 'Arise! / Be exalted'
a verdict on the proud — 'it was pride that caused their fall'

themes: hope spoken to a man already humbled

schools.summary: Gill asks where an 'island of innocent persons' is, prefers 'the innocent shall deliver the island' by counsel and prayer, but notes the word rendered 'island' is a negative particle ('not'), pointing to 'him that is not innocent.'

Keil and Delitzsch weigh 'the not-guiltless' — at first Job himself, the guilty who merited his suffering — and frame the third course of the controversy; Ellicott calls it 'undoubtedly' an error for 'him that is not innocent,' delivered by Job's clean hands as ten righteous would have saved Sodom, and hears a prophecy fulfilled when Eliphaz is himself pardoned through Job (ch. 42:8-9).

Clarke takes 'island' for an Arabic particle 'any' — 'he shall deliver every innocent person' — the word 'island' given up, and closes with a stern verdict on Eliphaz (scarcely one new maxim; bless God for Moses and the prophets); Wesley: God will deliver others for Job's sake, as the friends were (ch. 42:8).
Henry inclines to 'the innocent shall deliver the island' — a good man is a public good, and sinners fare the better for the saints among them.

debates.question: What does 'he shall deliver the island of the innocent' (i-naqi) mean?

sides.position: the innocent shall deliver the land/island by their prayers
the negative particle — 'him that is not innocent,' the guilty delivered for a righteous man's sake
'every innocent person' (Arabic ai, 'any')

outliers.note: Closes his account of Eliphaz with a stern verdict — a man who began with the bitterest charges and ended with commonplace exhortations has left scarcely one new maxim; 'blessed be God for Moses and the prophets.'

themes: deliver the island of the innocent
